questions.question: What is the core reason Parquet can avoid reading unrequested fields from a wide dataset?
options: Values for each column are stored in separate column chunks within a row group
Every Parquet file keeps all rows in a database index
The footer stores a complete copy of every value
Parquet converts every analytical query into a key-value lookup
questions.explanation: A row group contains one contiguous column chunk per column. A reader can use footer offsets to fetch only chunks for projected columns.

questions.question: A date filter does not overlap a row group's valid minimum and maximum date statistics. What may a capable reader do?
options: Skip that row group for the filter
Delete the row group from the file
Assume every row in the next group matches
Rewrite the file before returning results
questions.explanation: Non-overlapping statistics prove that the group cannot contain a match. An overlapping range only keeps the group as a candidate; row-level filtering may still be needed.

questions.question: Why did the ordered layout in the scan lab prune more row groups than the mixed-arrival layout?
options: Its row groups had narrow, non-overlapping date ranges
It stored fewer schema fields in the footer
It disabled compression for date columns
It guaranteed one row per data page
questions.explanation: Ordering correlated values narrows each group's min/max range. In the mixed layout, every range overlapped the filter, so statistics could not reject a group.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes encoding from compression in Parquet?
options: Encoding represents typed values; a codec can then compress the encoded page bytes
Encoding only encrypts the footer; compression changes column names
Encoding and compression are two names for the same mandatory algorithm
Compression runs before values are grouped into columns
questions.explanation: Parquet encodings exploit value structure, such as repeated dictionary IDs or numeric deltas. Compression codecs operate on the resulting page bytes.

questions.question: A producer renames customer_id to account_id in new files without a compatibility mapping. What does a name-based nullable union most likely expose?
options: Two sparse columns across old and new files
One automatically backfilled account_id column
A guaranteed field-ID match in every reader
A smaller footer with no schema change
questions.explanation: Renaming a file-local field does not move historical values. Name-based merging sees the old and new names as separate fields unless another layer maps or rewrites them.

questions.question: What is the most reliable way to choose file size, row-group size, sorting, and codec settings?
options: Measure representative writes and reads across every production engine
Use one universal row-group size for every object store and query
Choose the codec with the smallest sample regardless of CPU cost
Create one tiny file per event so every write is independent
questions.explanation: Format options interact with writer memory, object-store overhead, query shape, and reader feature support. Representative cross-engine measurement is the evidence that matters.
